title: Area IV review: Flight Operations Rules
intro: These questions mix all five Tasks of Area IV: right-of-way and collision avoidance, airport operations and runway safety, ATC clearances and the transponder, passengers and seat belts, and oxygen, aerobatics and parachutes. Many join two of them in one real flight.

questions.q: You are on left downwind at a non-towered airport, level at pattern altitude. A faster RV-7 comes up behind you on the same downwind at your altitude. What does 91.113 say?
options: The RV has the right-of-way because it is faster, so you should extend your downwind
You have the right-of-way; the RV pilot must alter course to the right and pass well clear
The RV should pass on your left, inside the pattern, so it stays close to the runway
Neither has the right-of-way until one of you turns final
questions.why: The aircraft being overtaken has the right-of-way, and the overtaking pilot alters course to the right to pass well clear [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(f)]]. In a left pattern the right side is the outside, so passing inside on your left is the wrong side. Speed gives no priority. The landing rule gives priority to aircraft on final or landing [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]], but neither of you is there yet, and the overtaking rule already applies. The AFH says a midair is most likely between two aircraft going the same direction [[24:170|AFH 8-6]].

questions.q: You enter left downwind at a non-towered airport where gliders and airplanes share the runway. A glider, lower and inside your pattern, turns base, and its path to final will cross ahead of yours. What applies?
options: You have the right-of-way, because you were on downwind first
The glider gets priority only once it is on final, under the landing rule
You have the right-of-way, because a powered airplane can maneuver more easily
The glider has the right-of-way; give way and do not pass over, under or ahead of it unless well clear
questions.why: A glider has the right-of-way over powered aircraft [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)(2)]], and AC 90-66C repeats this for non-towered airports [[17:16|AC 90-66C 12.2.1]]. The glider's priority comes from its category, anywhere in the pattern, not only from the landing rule. Expect it inside you: when both use one runway, the glider pattern is inside the powered pattern [[17:16|AC 90-66C 12.2.2]]. Giving way means not passing over, under or ahead unless well clear [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]].

questions.q: You fly west on VFR flight following, holding a ground track of 270. A strong wind from the north makes you crab, so your heading is 285. Approach calls traffic at 12 o'clock, 4 miles, eastbound. Where should you look first?
options: Left of the nose, because ATC gives the clock position along your track, not along your heading
Straight over the nose, because the controller corrects clock positions for wind
Right of the nose, toward the wind, because the crab pulls the traffic to the wind side
Nowhere yet: wait until the traffic shows on your ADS-B display
questions.why: The radar controller sees only your track, so 12 o'clock means straight ahead along your track, not over your nose [[33:216|AIM 4-1-15d]]. In AIM FIG 4-1-1, pilot B tracks west with the wind from the north and crabs the nose to the right of the track. B is told 12 o'clock but sees the traffic at 10 o'clock, to the left of the nose [[33:216|AIM 4-1-15d]]. Your heading of 285 is 15 degrees right of your 270 track, so the target sits about 15 degrees left of the nose, near 11:30; the AIM figure shows a larger crab. Waiting for the screen is wrong: an ADS-B display only helps you find traffic visually [[33:304|AIM 4-5-7e]], and some aircraft never show on it [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]].

questions.q: On a clear, moonless night you cruise a non-pressurized airplane at 9,500 ft for two hours with no oxygen on board. Which statement is correct?
options: It is legal, and below 12,000 ft altitude has no effect on a healthy pilot's vision
It is not legal: at night 91.211 requires the crew to use oxygen above 5,000 ft
It is legal under 91.211, but your night vision may already be degraded, so look about 10 degrees off a dim light
It is legal, and looking straight at a dim light is the best way to find traffic at night
questions.why: 91.211(a) starts at cabin pressure altitudes above 12,500 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)]]. Oxygen above 5,000 ft at night is an FAA recommendation, not the rule [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2a6]]. Night vision deteriorates at a cabin pressure altitude as low as 5,000 ft; only the other significant effects usually wait until 12,000 ft [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2a2]]. Staring is wrong: the center of your vision has a night blind spot 5 to 10 degrees wide, so look about 10 degrees above, below or beside a dim object [[16:13|AC 90-48E 13.1]].

questions.q: Before a VFR cross-country with a friend in the right seat, which plan best follows the AIM's collision avoidance advice?
options: Program the GPS en route to save ground time, and count on ADS-B In alerts while your head is down
Look outside in one long sweep each minute, then spend the rest of the time on the panel
Ask your friend not to speak at all during the flight, even about traffic, so you can concentrate
Load the route and frequencies before takeoff, keep panel time to about 4 to 5 seconds for every 16 outside, and ask your friend to help scan
questions.why: Studying charts and setting up frequencies before flight frees time for the scan [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]]. Time inside should be about 4 to 5 seconds for every 16 seconds outside, in short regular eye movements of no more than 10 degrees, each area viewed at least 1 second [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]]. The right seat passenger should scan too [[33:286|AIM 4-4-14c]]. An ADS-B display is not a collision avoidance system and does not relieve you of see and avoid [[33:304|AIM 4-5-7e]]. Quiet is fine in busy phases, but passengers should still speak up about a conflict [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b]].

questions.q: You arrive from the upwind side of a non-towered airport, field elevation 1,240 ft MSL, left traffic, no published pattern altitude. You fly a piston single, and no large or turbine aircraft use the field. Using the AFH's first upwind-side method, what do you fly?
options: Cross midfield at 2,740 ft MSL, go about 2 miles clear, descend to 2,240 ft MSL, then turn back to a 45 degree entry to downwind
Cross midfield at 2,740 ft MSL, then descend to 2,240 ft MSL while turning straight onto downwind
Cross midfield at 3,240 ft MSL, then descend while turning straight onto downwind
Skip the crossing and fly a straight-in, which gives you priority over pattern traffic
questions.why: Propeller airplanes fly the pattern 1,000 ft above the airport unless another altitude is published [[17:23|AC 90-66C A-5]]: 1,240 + 1,000 = 2,240 ft MSL. Cross midfield at least 500 ft above pattern altitude: 2,240 + 500 = 2,740 ft MSL (1,500 ft AGL). About 2 miles clear, descend to pattern altitude and turn to enter at 45 degrees to downwind [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]. 2,000 ft AGL is for fields with large or turbine aircraft [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]. The other two choices descend into the pattern, which the AC says not to do [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.3]]. A straight-in gets no priority [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11.1]].

questions.q: Your radio fails on the ramp of a towered airport and can't be fixed. You phone the tower, get approval to depart without a radio, and are told to watch for light signals. In daylight, which sequence lets you taxi and then take off, and how do you acknowledge?
options: Steady green to taxi, then flashing green for takeoff; acknowledge by blinking the landing light
Flashing green to taxi, then alternating red and green for takeoff; acknowledge by rocking the wings
Flashing white to taxi, then steady green for takeoff; no acknowledgment is possible on the ground
Flashing green to taxi, then steady green for takeoff; acknowledge by moving the ailerons or rudder
questions.why: Calling the tower by phone to ask to depart without two-way radio is what the AIM suggests [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13b]]. On the surface, flashing green means cleared to taxi and steady green means cleared for takeoff [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]]. Flashing white means return to your starting point, and alternating red and green means exercise extreme caution [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]]. By day you acknowledge by moving the ailerons or rudder; blinking the lights is the night method [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13e]].

questions.q: Ground says: "Skyhawk three four X, Runway three three, taxi via Alpha." Alpha meets the runway mid-field, where a red sign with white letters reads "15-33". What does the sign tell you, and may you roll onto the runway?
options: The Runway 33 threshold is to your left; the runway assignment lets you line up there
The Runway 33 threshold is to your right; stop at the holding position and get a clearance before entering
The Runway 33 threshold is to your right; the runway assignment lets you enter and taxi to it
It is a location sign showing you are on Runway 15-33; continue as cleared
questions.why: On a runway holding position sign the numbers match the thresholds: "15-33" means the Runway 15 threshold is to the left and the Runway 33 threshold is to the right [[33:162|AIM 2-3-8b1]]. White on red is a mandatory instruction sign [[19:13|AC 150/5340-18H xiii]]; a location sign is yellow on black [[33:165|AIM 2-3-9a1]]. Being assigned Runway 33 does not authorize you to enter or cross that departure runway at any point [[33:260|AIM 4-3-18a6]], and at a towered airport you need a clearance to operate on a runway [[60:454|14 CFR 91.129(i)]]. Hold with no part of the airplane past the holding position marking [[33:151|AIM 2-3-5a1]].

questions.q: You will taxi with two passengers at a busy towered airport. Which of these does NOT match AC 91-73B?
options: Brief the expected route, hold short lines, runway crossings and hot spots before you move
Ask passengers to keep quiet during taxi, but to speak up if they see a conflict
Program the GPS flight plan during the long straight taxi segments to save time
Write down a complex taxi clearance and follow your progress on the airport diagram
questions.why: Heads-down, high workload tasks such as programming a GPS belong before you begin to taxi; doing them while taxiing has significant safety implications [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d Note]]. The other three are AC advice: brief the route with hold short lines, runway crossings and hot spots, and remind occupants of the sterile cockpit while encouraging them to speak up about a conflict [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b]]. Write complex instructions down [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7e]] and follow your progress on the diagram [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7d(1)]]. The sterile period runs from preflight preparations until clear of the terminal area [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7c]].

questions.q: You depart a non-towered airport after sunset. Which lighting plan matches AC 91-73B and the AIM?
options: All exterior lights on to cross a runway; all lights except the landing lights on entering the runway; landing lights on as you start the takeoff roll
Position lights off until airborne, then landing lights on once clear of the pattern
Landing lights on from engine start, so other pilots can see you taxi
Exterior lights matter only at towered airports, where ATC watches for them
questions.why: Turn on all exterior lights when crossing a runway. On entering the runway for takeoff, turn on all lights except the landing lights, and turn the landing lights on when cleared for takeoff or, at an airport without a tower, as you begin the takeoff roll [[7:10|AC 91-73B 7h(2)]] [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24g]]. Turning landing lights on at engine start skips that step. Operation Lights On also encourages landing lights for takeoff and below 10,000 ft, especially within 10 miles of an airport [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24c]]. After sunset, position lights are required [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(a)(1)]], and lights help other pilots see you whether or not a tower is open.

questions.q: IFR in VMC on an assigned altitude, your oil pressure starts dropping. You turn toward a nearby airport and start down before ATC answers. ATC never gave you priority. What do 91.3 and 91.123 require afterward?
options: Send a detailed report to the ATC facility manager within 48 hours
Tell ATC about the deviation as soon as possible, and send a written report only if the Administrator asks for one
Nothing: an emergency cancels all reporting duties
Nothing, as long as you landed safely; reports are only for accidents
questions.why: In an in-flight emergency requiring immediate action you may deviate from part 91 as far as needed, and you send a written report if the Administrator asks [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(b), (c)]]. 91.123 allows deviating from a clearance in an emergency [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]], but you must notify ATC as soon as possible [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(c)]]. The 48-hour report is owed only when ATC gave you priority and asks for it [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(d)]], which did not happen here.

questions.q: ATC says: "Descend at pilot's discretion, maintain six thousand." You leave 9,000, level at 8,000 for smoother air, and then find that 9,000 was smoother still. What may you do?
options: Climb back to 9,000, since the whole descent was at your discretion
Stay at 8,000 as long as you like and continue to 6,000 later, but not climb back to 9,000 without a new clearance
Nothing: once you leave an altitude you must keep descending at 500 to 1,500 fpm
Climb back to 9,000 after telling ATC; no new clearance is needed
questions.why: "At pilot's discretion" lets you start when you like, descend at any rate, and level off temporarily at any intermediate altitude, but once you vacate an altitude you may not return to it [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10c]]. The 500 to 1,500 fpm guidance is for clearances without that phrase [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10d]]. Going back up would be a deviation from the clearance, which needs an amended clearance [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]].

questions.q: IFR, you break out into wide VFR conditions 40 miles from your destination, and minutes later all radios fail. The nearest airport, 5 miles away, is unsuitable for your airplane. What does the rule expect?
options: Land at the nearest airport, because the rule means as soon as possible
Climb back into the clouds and fly the rest of the filed route and altitudes
Squawk 7600, continue under VFR and land as soon as practicable, which need not be the nearest airport
Squawk 7500 and continue to your destination under IFR
questions.why: If the failure occurs in VFR conditions, continue the flight under VFR and land as soon as practicable [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(b)]]. The AIM says practicable does not mean as soon as possible; you need not land at an unsuitable airport or minutes short of your destination [[34:53|AIM 6-4-1c2]]. The IFR route and altitude rules are for IFR conditions or when (b) cannot be met [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(c)]]. The radio failure code is 7600 [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2a]]; 7500 means hijack [[34:52|AIM 6-3-4b]].

questions.q: Cruising VFR on flight following, you hear: "Cessna Four Five Kilo, squawk seven five zero zero." You have reported nothing unusual, and nothing is wrong. What should you do?
options: Set 7500 and read it back, because ATC instructions must be followed
Set 7700, since ATC asked for an emergency code
Refuse that code and tell the controller, because ATC never assigns 7500 unless the pilot first reports unlawful interference
Squawk 7600 and leave the frequency
questions.why: ATC will never assign 7500 without prior notice from the pilot that the aircraft is subject to unlawful interference, and the pilot should refuse it in any other case and tell the controller [[34:52|AIM 6-3-4b]]. Setting it would trip the special emergency indicator at every radar facility [[34:52|AIM 6-3-4b]]. When unsure of an ATC clearance, ask right away [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]]. 7700 is for distress or urgency [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2a]], and 7600 is for radio failure [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2a]]. When changing codes, avoid passing through 7500, 7600 or 7700 [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20e1]].

questions.q: IFR at FL270 in a pressurized single, on an assigned code, the cabin altitude warning sounds and the cabin altimeter is climbing. What is the best sequence?
options: Watch the cabin altimeter for a few minutes to see whether the cabin settles
Ask ATC for a descent clearance and wait for it before putting on the mask
Set 7700 at once, then put on the mask after ATC acknowledges
Mask on within 5 seconds with 100 percent oxygen, start down as the emergency requires, and tell ATC as soon as possible on your assigned code
questions.why: The cabin altitude warning in these airplanes activates at 10,000 ft cabin altitude [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9c]]. The AC's steps are don the mask in 5 seconds or less and breathe 100 percent oxygen, descend, preferably below 10,000 ft, and land as soon as possible [[11:27|AC 61-107B Table 2-6]]. Rapid loss of pressure cuts time of useful consciousness about in half [[11:29|AC 61-107B 2-7e(3)(a)]], and a slow decompression is at least as dangerous [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7e(3)]], so waiting is wrong. An emergency allows the deviation, and you notify ATC as soon as possible [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a), (c)]]. In contact with ATC, keep the assigned code unless told otherwise [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a2]].

questions.q: You plan 45 minutes at a cabin pressure altitude of 15,500 ft in a non-pressurized 4-seat airplane. You are the only required pilot. Your two passengers are a friend and a private pilot who is just riding along. Which plan meets 91.107 and 91.211?
options: Brief only the friend on the belts, since the pilot knows them; use oxygen yourself the whole time; provide oxygen for both passengers
Brief both on the belts; use oxygen yourself the whole time at that altitude; provide oxygen for both passengers
Brief both on the belts; use oxygen yourself only after the first 30 minutes at that altitude; provide oxygen for both passengers
Brief both on the belts; use oxygen yourself the whole time; provide oxygen for the friend only, since a rated pilot can look after himself
questions.why: Each person on board must be briefed on fastening and unfastening the belt and any shoulder harness, with no exception for pilots [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(1)]]. Above 14,000 ft cabin pressure altitude the required minimum flight crew uses oxygen during the entire time at those altitudes; the 30 minute allowance covers only 12,500 to 14,000 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(1), (2)]]. Above 15,000 ft each occupant must be provided with oxygen [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(3)]]. A pilot riding along is an occupant like anyone else, so leaving him out is wrong. The rule says provided, so it does not make every passenger breathe it.

questions.q: A child's aunt, chosen by the parents, brings an approved and correctly labeled child seat. She wants it strapped to the side-facing bench in the back. What does 91.107 allow?
options: Nothing: only a parent or legal guardian may accompany a child in a child seat
The bench is fine if the child is under 2 and the aunt also holds the child
The bench is fine, since any approved seat or berth may hold a child seat
Not on that bench: the child seat must be secured to an approved forward-facing seat or berth
questions.why: An approved child restraint may be used when the child is with a parent, guardian or an attendant the parent or guardian designated, and the seat is properly secured to an approved forward-facing seat or berth [[60:442|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(iii)]]. So the designated aunt is fine, but the side-facing bench is not. A lap child must be under 2 and may not use any restraining device [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(i)]], so holding the child in the seat on a lap does not work either.

questions.q: In smooth cruise on a Part 91 flight, you are the only pilot and your passenger is in the back. Both of you want to unbuckle and stretch. Which is correct?
options: You may both unbuckle, because belts are required only for surface movement, takeoff and landing
Your passenger may unbuckle, but you must keep your safety belt fastened while at your station
You may unbuckle while the autopilot flies, since you stay at your station
Neither may unbuckle, because 91.107 requires passenger belts for the whole flight
questions.why: A required flight crewmember keeps the safety belt fastened while at the station during takeoff, landing and en route; the shoulder harness rule covers takeoff and landing [[60:441|14 CFR 91.105]]. People covered by 91.105 are not covered by the passenger rule [[60:442|14 CFR 91.107(b)]], which ties passenger belts to surface movement, takeoff and landing [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)]]. An autopilot does not change 91.105. Application: an unbelted passenger has no protection if turbulence hits; in moderate turbulence occupants feel definite strains against their belts [[34:106|AIM TBL 7-1-11]].

questions.q: Just after liftoff, the passenger door pops open with a loud bang. Your passenger starts to unbuckle to grab it. What should you do?
options: Tell the passenger to stay belted and leave the door, keep flying the airplane, and land when practicable to close it on the ground
Have the passenger unbuckle and pull it shut while you are still low and slow
Unbuckle yourself and reach across to close it while the airplane is trimmed
Make the door your first job, since the airplane is in danger until it is closed
questions.why: The AFH says a door opening is seldom a threat by itself; the danger is the pilot's reaction, so concentrate on flying the airplane [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]. Do not release the belt or harness to reach the door. Leave it, land as soon as practicable and close it on the ground [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]. The passenger also must stay belted for takeoff and landing [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)]]. The passenger briefing includes how to secure and open the exit doors [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

questions.q: You fly a pressurized single at FL260 with the cabin holding 9,000 ft and three passengers aboard. What does 91.211 require?
options: The crew must use oxygen the whole time, because the airplane is above 14,000 ft
Nothing, because a pressurized cabin at 9,000 ft removes every oxygen requirement
One pilot at the controls must wear and use a sealed oxygen mask
No crew oxygen use under 91.211(a), but at least a 10-minute supply for each occupant must be available for a descent after pressure loss
questions.why: The 91.211(a) steps are measured in cabin pressure altitude, and 9,000 ft is below all of them [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)]]. Above FL250 in a pressurized cabin, though, at least a 10-minute supply for each occupant must be available for a descent forced by loss of pressurization [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(b)(1)(i)]]. The sealed mask rule starts above FL350 [[60:492|14 CFR 91.211(b)(1)(ii)]]. Even pressurized airplanes need oxygen aboard, because decompression is always possible [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9c]].

questions.q: On a winter flight at 7,500 ft with the cabin heater on, you notice a headache and drowsiness. What type of hypoxia is most likely, and what should you do?
options: Hypemic hypoxia from carbon monoxide: shut off the heater, open the air vents, and get medical help if symptoms continue after landing
Hypoxic hypoxia from the altitude: climb to smoother air
Histotoxic hypoxia from the cold: turn the heater up
Stagnant hypoxia from the cold: keep the heater on and descend
questions.why: Most light airplane heaters pass air over the exhaust manifold. Headache, drowsiness or dizziness with the heater on means suspect carbon monoxide, shut off the heater and open the vents, and seek treatment if symptoms are severe or continue after landing [[34:184|AIM 8-1-4]]. Carbon monoxide causes hypemic hypoxia, where the blood cannot carry enough oxygen [[1:425|PHAK 17-3]]. Altitude is a poor fit: other significant effects of altitude hypoxia usually do not occur below 12,000 ft in a healthy pilot [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2a2]]. Histotoxic hypoxia comes from alcohol, narcotics or poisons [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].

questions.q: You reach a charted aerobatic practice area over open country, far from airways and airport surface areas. You are at 3,000 ft AGL, but haze holds flight visibility to 2.5 SM. May you start your aerobatic routine?
options: Yes: inside a charted aerobatic practice area, the 91.303 limits do not apply
Yes: the 3 SM limit applies only over congested areas
No: 91.303 bans aerobatics when flight visibility is less than 3 SM, and the charted area does not change that
Yes, if you stay above 1,500 ft AGL and make clearing turns first
questions.why: No aerobatic flight when flight visibility is less than 3 SM; that limit applies anywhere, not only over congested areas [[60:505|14 CFR 91.303(f)]]. The 1,500 ft AGL floor is a separate limit, so meeting it does not cure the visibility [[60:505|14 CFR 91.303(e)]]. The chart legend shows the practice area symbol only; it does not say the area changes 91.303 [[2:46|Chart Users' Guide p 46]]. Haze also makes traffic hard to see, even at 5 sm visibility [[16:7|AC 90-48E 8.1.9 to 8.1.10]].

questions.q: Your CFI gives you the spin training the regulations require for the flight instructor certificate you are working toward. Neither of you wears a parachute. What does 91.307 say?
options: It is allowed: 91.307(c) does not apply to spins required by the regulations for a certificate when given by a CFI
It is not allowed: spins exceed 30 degrees nose-down, so each occupant needs a parachute
It is allowed only on the practical test, with an examiner aboard
It is allowed only if parachutes packed within 180 days are stowed aboard
questions.why: Without approved parachutes on each occupant, a pilot carrying anyone other than a crewmember may not exceed 60 degrees of bank or 30 degrees of pitch [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(c)]]. That paragraph does not apply to flight tests, or to spins and other maneuvers required by the regulations for a certificate or rating when given by a CFI or by an ATP instructing under 61.67 [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(d)]]. So the training is covered without an examiner. The 180-day packing rule is for parachutes carried for emergency use, and stowing one is not wearing one [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(a)]]. Before spin training, the AFH says to review the current parachute rules [[24:128|AFH 5-23]].

questions.q: Crossing a ridge in daylight, your cabin altitude is 13,800 ft for 25 minutes. You feel sharp, and your pulse oximeter reading looks normal. Which is correct?
options: It is not legal: the crew must use oxygen the whole time above 12,500 ft
It is legal and safe: a normal oximeter reading proves you are not hypoxic
91.211 does not require oxygen yet, but the FAA encourages it above 10,000 ft by day, and neither feeling fine nor the oximeter rules out impairment
It is legal for 30 minutes; after that, each passenger must be provided with oxygen
questions.why: Between 12,500 and 14,000 ft cabin altitude, the crew needs oxygen only for the part of the flight there that is more than 30 minutes [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(1)]]. The FAA encourages oxygen above 10,000 ft by day [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2a6]]. The AC calls it a dangerous misconception that hypoxia symptoms are easy to recognize in time [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7d(2)(e)]], and warns against using a pulse oximeter as the sole indicator [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7d(2)(f)]]. Passengers must be provided with oxygen only above 15,000 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(3)]].
